subsection: 3. The Nazi state in peace, 1933-1939, and Hitler's foreign policy

notes.h: Hitler's aims and the start of his chancellorship, January 1933
notes.b: Everything the Nazi state did between 1933 and 1939 makes sense only against what Hitler wanted and the position he started from. He came to power through a deal with conservatives, but he had a programme that he had already written down.
points: Hitler was appointed Chancellor on 30 January 1933 by President Hindenburg, at the head of a coalition. Only three Nazis (Hitler, Frick and Göring) sat in the first cabinet, so Papen, the Vice-Chancellor, and the conservatives expected to control him.

In Mein Kampf (two volumes, 1925 and 1926, mostly written in Landsberg prison after the Munich Putsch) Hitler set out his aims: overturn Versailles, unite all Germans in one state, win Lebensraum (living space) in the east, and fight a racial struggle.

The Treaty of Versailles (1919) limited the German army to 100,000 men and banned conscription, an air force, tanks and submarines, which is why rearmament was Hitler's first goal. The Rhineland was demilitarised and the Saar placed under League of Nations rule for 15 years from 1920.

Versailles also forbade union (Anschluss) with Austria, made Danzig a Free City under the League, and used the Polish Corridor to separate East Prussia from the rest of Germany. Each of these became a Hitler target between 1933 and 1939.
While Germany was weak, Hitler was cautious: he needed time to rebuild the army and economy, so his first steps were presented as demands for fair treatment, not as plans for conquest.
notes.tip: For the Ordinary Level foreign policy paragraph, a run of dated steps earns the marks. In the Higher Level essay on how far Hitler's foreign policy caused the war, weigh Versailles as one of the other factors alongside his aims and the stages 1933-39.

notes.h: Consolidating power, 1933: the Reichstag fire to the Enabling Act
notes.b: Within months of his appointment Hitler removed the legal and political limits on his power, using emergency decrees, intimidation and a vote of the Reichstag itself. Each step built on the one before.
points: The Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933 was blamed on a Communist plot, because Marinus van der Lubbe, a young Dutch communist (later executed), was found in the building. This gave the Nazis the excuse they needed to attack their left-wing opponents.

The Decree for the Protection of People and State (the Reichstag Fire Decree) of 28 February 1933 suspended freedom of speech, press and assembly and allowed arrest without trial, so opponents could be locked up with no legal protection.
Thousands of Communists were arrested after the fire, and the Communist Party was effectively destroyed in early 1933, removing one of the Nazis' main rivals before the next vote.

In the election of 5 March 1933, despite terror and propaganda, the Nazis won only about 44 per cent of the vote. They had a majority only with their Nationalist (DNVP) allies, so Hitler still needed another way to rule freely.

The Enabling Act of 23 March 1933 (formally the Law for the Removal of the Distress of People and Reich) let the cabinet make laws without the Reichstag, even ones departing from the constitution, for four years.

The Act passed 444 to 94. The Communist deputies had been arrested or had fled, the Catholic Centre Party voted for it, and only the Social Democrats voted against, which shows how far intimidation had worked.
Do not mix up the two measures: the Reichstag Fire Decree suspended people's rights, while the Enabling Act removed the Reichstag's law-making role.
notes.tip: Examiners ask you to distinguish the Reichstag Fire Decree (28 February) from the Enabling Act (23 March): the first suspended rights, the second removed the Reichstag's law-making role. Give both dates and what each did.

notes.h: Gleichschaltung and the one-party state, 1933-1934
notes.b: After the Enabling Act Hitler used Gleichschaltung (coordination: bringing every institution into line with Nazi aims) to take over the rest of German life. It ended in a state where only one party and one organisation for workers were allowed.
points: Reich governors (Reichsstatthalter) were appointed over the German states in April 1933, and the Law for the Reconstruction of the Reich of 30 January 1934 abolished the state parliaments, so power was concentrated in Berlin.

The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service of 7 April 1933 removed Jews and political opponents from the civil service. This put the officials who ran the country under Nazi control and made loyalty the test for a job.
Gleichschaltung also brought the courts, universities and cultural bodies under Nazi control, which meant that teaching, law and the arts could no longer act independently of the regime.

On 2 May 1933 the SA and SS occupied trade union offices and the unions were dissolved. Their members were not abolished by law but seized and absorbed, with workers then pushed into the German Labour Front, set up in May 1933 under Robert Ley.

The Law against the Formation of New Parties of 14 July 1933 made the NSDAP the only legal party. The Communists and Social Democrats had already been banned, and the other parties dissolved themselves in June and July 1933.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph on how Hitler consolidated power in 1933-34, give dated steps and say what each did. Say the unions were seized by the SA and SS on 2 May 1933, not abolished by a law.

notes.h: The Night of the Long Knives, 1934
notes.b: By 1934 Hitler's remaining rival at the heart of the movement was his own storm-troop army, the SA. Removing its leadership in one weekend won him the army's support and cleared the way to supreme power.
points: Ernst Röhm, the SA chief of staff, led an organisation of several million members by 1934, far more than the 100,000-man army. He talked of a "second revolution" and wanted the SA to form the core of a new people's army.

Conservatives were alarmed by SA violence. Vice-Chancellor Papen's Marburg speech of 17 June 1934 criticised that violence and the calls for a second revolution, adding to the pressure on Hitler to act.
Between 30 June and 2 July 1934, Hitler ordered the murder of Röhm and other SA leaders. The killings were carried out by the SS and Gestapo with army help.

Hitler also used the purge to settle other scores: Gregor Strasser (a former Nazi leader), Kurt von Schleicher (former Chancellor) and his wife, Gustav von Kahr, Erich Klausener and Edgar Jung (author of the Marburg speech) were killed.
At least 85 people were killed, possibly more, because the true total is uncertain.
On 3 July 1934 the Law on Measures of State Self-Defence declared the killings legal after the event, which gave murder a cover of legality.
The army leadership, under Defence Minister Werner von Blomberg, approved the purge in return for the removal of the SA as a rival force, which tied the army to Hitler.
notes.tip: Use the law's name when you describe the legalisation (the Law on Measures of State Self-Defence, 3 July 1934) and give the toll as at least 85, possibly more, not as an exact figure.

notes.h: Hitler becomes Führer: the Führer state
notes.b: Hindenburg's death gave Hitler the last piece of formal power. From then on the state rested on his person, and the law, the army and the party all swore obedience to him.
points: President Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934. The offices of President and Chancellor were merged and Hitler took the title Führer and Reich Chancellor. He was never called President. A plebiscite on 19 August 1934 approved the change, with about 90 per cent in favour.
On 2 August 1934 soldiers swore an oath of unconditional obedience to Hitler personally, as Führer, rather than to the constitution. This tied the armed forces to Hitler personally.
The Führer principle (Führerprinzip) meant authority flowed from the top down, with absolute obedience upward, and propaganda built a cult of Hitler's personal leadership around it.

In practice the state was a polycracy: overlapping party and state bodies (ministries, Gauleiters, the SS, the Four Year Plan office) competed for power and for Hitler's favour. This rivalry meant decisions could be chaotic.

A dictatorship is rule by one person or party without legal limits or free elections. By August 1934 Hitler had removed the Reichstag's law-making role, rival parties and independent organisations and so fitted this definition.
notes.tip: Define the Führer principle and polycracy separately: the first means orders from the top, the second means rival agencies competing for Hitler's favour. Use both in essays on how Hitler kept control.

notes.h: Terror and the police state: the SS, Gestapo and SD
notes.b: The regime did not rely on consent alone. A police system outside the law, led by Heinrich Himmler, gave it the power to detain anyone it chose.
points: Heinrich Himmler was Reichsführer-SS (head of the SS, the party's elite force) from 1929. By 1934 he controlled the political police of almost all the states, and in June 1936 he became Chief of German Police, which merged party and state police power in his hands.
Reinhard Heydrich led the SD (Sicherheitsdienst), the SS Security Service, which watched for opponents and gathered intelligence on the population.
The Gestapo (Secret State Police) was founded in April 1933 in Prussia by Hermann Göring. Himmler and Heydrich took it over in April 1934.

The Gestapo could arrest people without trial or appeal, a procedure the regime called protective custody (Schutzhaft). Because there was no legal challenge, nobody could force the police to explain or end a detention.

Historians such as Robert Gellately have shown that the Gestapo was small and relied heavily on denunciations by ordinary Germans. Its reach therefore depended partly on people reporting their neighbours, not on police numbers alone.

Do not confuse the organisations: the SA were the brownshirts under Röhm, sidelined after 1934; the SS was the party elite force under Himmler; the SD was SS intelligence under Heydrich; the Gestapo was the secret state police.
notes.tip: Keep the four organisations apart: SA (Röhm), SS (Himmler), SD (Heydrich) and Gestapo (secret state police). Mixing them up is a common mistake in terror questions.

notes.h: Terror and the police state: camps and courts
notes.b: Detention and the courts completed the system. Camps held people the regime wanted out of sight, and the courts were changed so political cases could be decided without legal protection.
points: Dachau, near Munich, opened in March 1933 and was the first concentration camp run by the SS and the model for later camps. The SA also ran makeshift early camps in 1933, which is why Dachau is called the first SS camp.
Other camps followed: Sachsenhausen in 1936 and Buchenwald in 1937, so the system grew as the regime's controls hardened.

The first prisoners were political opponents such as Communists, trade unionists and Social Democrats. Later Jehovah's Witnesses, "asocials", homosexuals and Jews were held too, so the camps widened as the idea of who threatened the community widened.

Special Courts (Sondergerichte) were set up in March 1933 and the People's Court (Volksgerichtshof) in 1934 for treason cases. Political verdicts came with little legal protection for defendants, so courts reinforced terror instead of limiting it.
notes.tip: For terror essays, name the SS, Gestapo, camps and courts with a date each. Say Dachau was the first SS-run camp, not simply the first camp.

notes.h: Economic recovery and rearmament, 1933-1935
notes.b: The regime's popularity depended on jobs, and its foreign aims depended on arms. Its economic policy tried to deliver both, and hide how much it was spending on rearmament.
points: Hjalmar Schacht was Reichsbank president from March 1933 and Economics Minister from August 1934. He financed rearmament through Mefo bills, credit notes issued through a dummy company (Mefo) to pay arms firms, which kept military spending off the budget.

The New Plan of September 1934 controlled foreign trade through bilateral trade agreements and exchange controls (limits on buying foreign money), which gave priority to imports of raw materials for rearmament.

Public works, including autobahns, housing and military building, created jobs. The first autobahn section, Frankfurt to Darmstadt, opened in May 1935. The Nazis expanded and publicised the autobahns, but plans and a first stretch (Cologne to Bonn, 1932) predate 1933.

The Reich Labour Service (RAD) became compulsory for young men in June 1935, with six months' work, and conscription was reintroduced in March 1935. Both took young men out of the job market, which helped to lower the unemployment figures.
notes.tip: Describe Schacht with his tools: Mefo bills hid military spending and the New Plan put raw materials for arms first. Do not claim the Nazis invented the autobahns.

notes.h: Unemployment, the Four Year Plan and the limits of recovery
notes.b: Unemployment fell dramatically, but the figures hide a more complicated story, and from 1936 the economy was steered openly towards war.
points: Registered unemployment was about six million in January 1933 and under one million by 1937. By 1938-39 labour shortages had replaced unemployment, because rearmament and conscription absorbed workers.
The figures hide a lot: women and Jews were removed from them, conscription and the Labour Service took men out of the labour market, wages were held down and there were no free unions to bargain.
Recovery had begun before 1933 and world trade was recovering, so Nazi policy alone did not end the Depression in Germany. Historians therefore debate how much credit the regime deserves.

The Four Year Plan, announced in September 1936 with Hermann Göring as Plenipotentiary, aimed to have the army ready for action and the economy fit for war within four years. This priority is often paraphrased as guns before butter.

It also aimed at autarky (self-sufficiency, so Germany would not depend on imports in wartime), through synthetic oil from coal, synthetic rubber (buna) and the state-owned Reichswerke Hermann Göring (1937), which mined low-grade German iron ore.
The plan missed its targets, and Germany still relied on imports in 1939.

Schacht resigned as Economics Minister in November 1937 after clashing with Göring over the pace and cost of rearmament. He was dismissed from the Reichsbank in January 1939, and by 1939 the economy was strained.
notes.tip: For judgement questions on the economy, pair the achievement (unemployment cut from about six million to under one million, recovery, rearmament) with the limits (hidden unemployment, controlled wages, strain by 1939).

notes.h: The Volksgemeinschaft: workers and youth
notes.b: The Volksgemeinschaft (people's community) was the idea of a racially pure national community that stood above class. The regime tried to win workers and shape children so that they would belong to it.
points: The German Labour Front under Robert Ley replaced the free unions, so workers had an organisation controlled by the party instead of one that could bargain for them.

Its Strength Through Joy (Kraft durch Freude) section, set up in November 1933, offered cheap holidays, cruises, concerts, theatre and sport, so workers felt rewarded. Its Beauty of Labour section improved factory canteens, lighting and washrooms.
The Volkswagen ("people's car", the KdF-Wagen) scheme had workers pay weekly instalments, but the factory turned to war production and no savers received a car.

The Hitler Youth, led by Baldur von Schirach (Reich Youth Leader from 1933), had four sections: the Jungvolk (boys 10-14), the Hitler Youth (boys 14-18), the Jungmädelbund (girls 10-14) and the League of German Girls, the BDM (girls 14-18).

The Hitler Youth Law of 1 December 1936 made the Hitler Youth the only legal youth organisation, and membership became compulsory from 1939, so by the end of the decade almost no young person could avoid its training.

Schools taught racial science and nationalist history, and textbooks were rewritten. Teachers were pressed to join the National Socialist Teachers' League, and teachers who were Jewish or politically unreliable were dismissed.
notes.tip: When asked about Nazi control of youth, name the organisation, its leader and the 1936 law, and add schools: textbooks, racial science and the Teachers' League.

notes.h: The Volksgemeinschaft: women, outsiders and consent
notes.b: The national community was defined by who it left out as much as who it included. Women were given a fixed role, those judged outsiders were excluded, and the regime relied on consent as well as terror.
points: Nazi ideology assigned women the roles of wife and mother, often summed up as "Kinder, Küche, Kirche" (children, kitchen, church). The slogan is older than the Nazis, who did not coin it, but it describes their policy.

Marriage loans from 1933 (Law for the Reduction of Unemployment, June 1933) gave 1,000 marks, with a quarter cancelled for each child born. The wife was expected to give up work, which also freed jobs for men.
The Cross of Honour of the German Mother, instituted in December 1938, rewarded large families: bronze for four children, silver for six and gold for eight.
Married women were pushed out of civil service posts from 1933, and from 1936 women could not be judges or public prosecutors. But labour shortages in the late 1930s drew many women back into work.

The regime excluded those it judged inferior. The law of 14 July 1933 on hereditarily diseased offspring led to about 400,000 people being forcibly sterilised by 1945, and the Nuremberg Laws of 15 September 1935 took citizenship from Jews and banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and Germans.
Opponents and "asocials" were sent to camps, so belonging to the community depended on conforming.

The regime was also popular. Jobs, order and foreign successes won consent, while opposition was limited and mostly passive. After the Anschluss, the slogan "One People, One Reich, One Leader" summed up the mood.
notes.tip: Do not say women were banned from medicine or law in 1933. Use the dates: civil service posts from 1933, judges and prosecutors from 1936. Mention both consent and terror when asked about how the regime kept control.

notes.h: Hitler's early foreign policy, 1933-1935
notes.b: Hitler's first foreign moves rejected the Versailles restrictions step by step. Each time the western powers protested but did not act, which taught him how far he could go.
points: On 14 October 1933 Germany left the Geneva Disarmament Conference and the League of Nations, claiming unequal treatment. A plebiscite in November 1933 approved the move, with about 95 per cent in favour.
The German-Polish non-aggression pact of 26 January 1934, for ten years.

On 25 July 1934 Austrian Nazis murdered Chancellor Dollfuss in a failed coup in Vienna. Mussolini moved troops to the Brenner Pass, so Hitler backed off and disowned the coup. Kurt Schuschnigg succeeded Dollfuss.
The Saar, governed by the League since 1920, held a plebiscite on 13 January 1935 in which about 90 per cent voted to return to Germany. It was reunited on 1 March 1935, a major propaganda success.

In March 1935 Göring revealed the existence of the Luftwaffe (the German air force) to foreign journalists, and on 16 March Hitler announced conscription, with the army to grow to 36 divisions (about 550,000 men). Both breached Versailles.

The Stresa Front of Britain, France and Italy condemned German rearmament in April 1935 and promised to uphold Locarno and Austrian independence, but took no effective action and broke down after Italy invaded Abyssinia in October 1935.

The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 18 June 1935 allowed Germany a surface fleet up to 35 per cent the size of the British. Britain accepted it without consulting France, so a Versailles limit was broken with British consent.
The agreement gave Hitler the diplomatic recognition he had sought and weakened the united front against him, which encouraged him to test the western powers further.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph on foreign policy, a run of dated steps (League 1933, Saar and conscription 1935, Naval Agreement) earns the marks. Give the Saar result as about 90 per cent, and keep the Luftwaffe revelation separate from the 16 March conscription announcement.

notes.h: Expansion in Europe, 1936-1938: the Rhineland, the Axis and Austria
notes.b: From 1936 Hitler moved from undoing Versailles to open expansion, supported by new friends and a growing army. The western powers' failure to resist the Rhineland set the pattern for what followed.
points: On 7 March 1936 German troops reoccupied the demilitarised Rhineland (the reoccupation), breaking Versailles and the Locarno Treaties of 1925. France, in the middle of an election campaign, and Britain did not resist; the League only condemned it. Hitler offered new peace pacts the same day.
It was a gamble, and the generals were nervous, but its success increased Hitler's popularity at home and his confidence that Britain and France would not fight.

The Rome-Berlin Axis (agreed in October 1936 and named by Mussolini in a speech on 1 November 1936) and the Anti-Comintern Pact between Germany and Japan (25 November 1936, with Italy joining in November 1937) aligned Germany with Italy and Japan.
The German Condor Legion (air and ground units) fought for Franco in the Spanish Civil War from 1936 to 1939 and bombed Guernica in April 1937.

At the Hossbach meeting of 5 November 1937 Hitler told Blomberg, Fritsch, Raeder, Göring and Neurath that Germany's need for space could be solved only by force, at the latest by 1943-45 and earlier if chances arose, starting with Austria and Czechoslovakia.
The minutes were written up days later by Colonel Friedrich Hossbach, so the meeting is known as the Hossbach Memorandum.

In February 1938 Blomberg and Fritsch were removed after personal scandals. Hitler took personal command of the armed forces through a new High Command (OKW), and Joachim von Ribbentrop replaced Neurath as Foreign Minister.

The Anschluss followed: Hitler pressed Schuschnigg at Berchtesgaden in February 1938 to admit Austrian Nazis, including Seyss-Inquart as Interior Minister. Schuschnigg announced a plebiscite for 13 March, cancelled it under pressure and resigned on 11 March; German troops entered Austria on 12 March 1938.
notes.tip: The Anschluss date is 12 March 1938 (troops crossing), with Schuschnigg resigning on 11 March. Do not mix up the Berchtesgaden meeting with Schuschnigg (February 1938) and the one with Chamberlain (15 September 1938).

notes.h: The Sudeten crisis and the Munich Agreement, 1938
notes.b: After Austria, Hitler turned to Czechoslovakia. The Sudeten crisis showed how far Britain and France would go to avoid war and how Czechoslovakia was left to pay the price.
points: Austria was declared part of the Reich on 13 March 1938, and a plebiscite on 10 April 1938 showed over 99 per cent approval, a result produced in an atmosphere of Nazi control.

Konrad Henlein's Sudeten German Party, backed and funded by Berlin, demanded autonomy and then union with Germany for the three million Sudeten Germans, giving Hitler a pretext to threaten Czechoslovakia.
Chamberlain flew to meet Hitler at Berchtesgaden on 15 September 1938 and again at Bad Godesberg on 22 September, where Hitler raised his demands to immediate occupation.

The Munich conference met on 29 September 1938 and the agreement was signed in the early hours of 30 September by Chamberlain, Daladier (France), Hitler and Mussolini. Czechoslovakia was not represented and the Soviet Union, which had a treaty with Czechoslovakia, was not invited.
Czechoslovakia had to hand over the Sudetenland to Germany between 1 and 10 October 1938, and lost its frontier fortifications, leaving it defenceless.
Chamberlain and Hitler also signed a declaration that Britain and Germany would never go to war again. On his return Chamberlain said it was "peace for our time".
Churchill told the Commons in October 1938 that Munich was "a total and unmitigated defeat".
notes.tip: Examiners ask for the Munich signatories and who was excluded: Chamberlain, Daladier, Hitler and Mussolini signed; Czechoslovakia and the USSR were left out. The quotation is "peace for our time", not "peace in our time".

notes.h: From Prague to war, 1939
notes.b: Hitler's seizure of Prague in 1939 broke the logic of appeasement, and within months the road to war was open.
points: On 15 March 1939 German troops occupied Prague. Bohemia and Moravia became the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, and Slovakia, which declared independence on 14 March, became a German client state.
Memel was taken from Lithuania in March 1939, and Italy invaded Albania in April 1939.
Prague broke the Munich promises and was Hitler's first seizure of non-German land. It ended the belief that his claims were limited to Germans and led Britain to abandon appeasement.

Hitler demanded Danzig and a road and rail link across the Polish Corridor. Britain announced a guarantee of Polish independence on 31 March 1939, with France joining it, and the Anglo-Polish alliance followed on 25 August 1939.

The Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact (the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact) was signed in Moscow on 23 August 1939 by Ribbentrop and Molotov. It promised ten years of non-aggression, and a secret protocol divided Poland and placed the Baltic states and Bessarabia in spheres of influence.
The pact removed the danger of a war on two fronts and was surprising because the two regimes were ideological enemies.
Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war on 3 September.
notes.tip: A cartoon of the Nazi-Soviet Pact: say who the figures are, when and where it was signed, what the symbols mean, why it was surprising (ideological enemies) and what followed (Poland 1939; Germany invaded the USSR in 1941).

notes.h: Ideology, Lebensraum and the plan-or-opportunism debate
notes.b: Hitler's foreign policy was driven by racial ideas and by the goal of Lebensraum in the east. Historians argue over whether this meant a plan for war from the start or opportunism.
points: Lebensraum (living space) was Hitler's goal: Germany needed land in Eastern Europe, to be settled by a racially pure population, with the Slavs to be subjugated. This made war with the east, not just revision of Versailles, the aim.
Herrenvolk (master race) was the idea that Germanic people were racially superior. It underpinned both domestic policy and plans for the conquest and resettlement of Eastern Europe.
Totalitarianism and dictatorship: Hitler's ideology claimed to reach every part of life, which is why the regime tried to control work, schools and families as well as politics.
Appeasement was British and French policy to satisfy Germany's grievances through concessions, based on the belief that Versailles had been unfair and that war must be avoided.

Historians disagree on whether Hitler planned a general war from 1933 or responded to opportunities. Trevor-Roper argued Hitler pursued consistent war aims set out in Mein Kampf (the plan or programme view).
A.J.P. Taylor's The Origins of the Second World War (1961) argued that Hitler was an opportunist with traditional German aims and that the war was a blunder. The book was widely attacked.
The terms intentionalist (Hitler's plan) and functionalist (circumstances and rival agencies) are borrowed from the wider debate about the Nazi state.
notes.tip: For foreign policy, frame the argument as plan versus opportunism: say the intentionalist plan view and Taylor's opportunism, then give a balanced verdict: fixed long-term aims, opportunist timing and methods.

notes.h: Appeasement
notes.b: Appeasement was the policy of giving way to Hitler's demands to keep the peace. It was supported for several reasons and judged very differently at the time and afterwards.
points: Britain and France appeased Hitler for several reasons: guilt over Versailles, a horror of another war, a fear of bombing, rearmament that was not ready, reluctant dominions, a belief that communism was the greater threat, and the cost to the economy.

Neville Chamberlain, Prime Minister from May 1937 (succeeding Stanley Baldwin) to May 1940, was its main practitioner, so Munich is linked to his name. Churchill, out of office in the 1930s, was its main critic.
At the time appeasement was popular: Chamberlain was cheered on his return from Munich.
Later it was condemned: the pamphlet Guilty Men (1940), by "Cato" (Michael Foot and others), blamed the appeasers, but some historians defend it as buying time to rearm.
notes.tip: Do not blame Baldwin for Munich: Chamberlain was Prime Minister from 1937 to 1940. Be ready for contemporary versus later views.

notes.h: The Nazi state in war, 1939-1945 (outline)
notes.b: The war gave the regime new radical powers, and Germany's economy and society were geared to total war.
points: Albert Speer, Hitler's architect, became Minister for Armaments and Munitions in February 1942 after the death of Fritz Todt. Arms output rose sharply until 1944 despite bombing.
After the surrender at Stalingrad, Goebbels called for total war in his Sportpalast speech in Berlin on 18 February 1943. In January 1943 women aged 17 to 45 were required to register for war work.
Millions of foreign forced labourers and prisoners of war worked in Germany by 1944.

On 20 July 1944 Colonel Claus Schenk von Stauffenberg planted a bomb at Hitler's headquarters, the Wolf's Lair near Rastenburg, East Prussia. Hitler was only injured, the coup in Berlin collapsed that night and Stauffenberg was shot.
Thousands were arrested and many executed after the July plot.
Hitler stayed in command to the end and killed himself in his Berlin bunker on 30 April 1945.
notes.tip: For the July plot, name Stauffenberg, the Wolf's Lair and the date, and say Hitler survived. Say registration for women aged 17 to 45, not conscription.

notes.h: Key personality: Adolf Hitler (the Nazi state and foreign policy, 1933-1939)
notes.b: Hitler's rule from 1933 to 1939 combined a consolidated dictatorship at home with a foreign policy of rearmament, expansion and war. He directed each stage himself.
points: Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 at Braunau am Inn, Austria. He served in a Bavarian regiment from 1914 to 1918 and won the Iron Cross First Class in 1918.
He led the Nazi Party from July 1921, attempted the Munich (Beer Hall) Putsch in November 1923, wrote Mein Kampf in Landsberg prison in 1924, and became Chancellor on 30 January 1933.

From 1933 to 1939 he built a dictatorship, rearmed, left the League, took the Rhineland, achieved the Anschluss with Austria, received the Sudetenland under the Munich Agreement, occupied Prague and invaded Poland.
He set the aims and took the key decisions on the purge, the Rhineland, the Anschluss, Czechoslovakia and Poland. He was a participant who directed each stage, not a witness.
His style of rule was to rise late, avoid paperwork and encourage rivalry between subordinates, who competed to anticipate his wishes: what Ian Kershaw calls "working towards the Führer".

At home, he was popular after the Saar, the Rhineland and the Anschluss. Abroad, David Lloyd George visited him in September 1936 and praised him, and many saw a reasonable revisionist, but Churchill warned repeatedly of German rearmament and saw a threat.

Historians' views have changed. Alan Bullock (Hitler: A Study in Tyranny, 1952) saw an opportunist adventurer seeking power, a view later revised. Trevor-Roper stressed consistent war aims, and Taylor argued Hitler was an opportunist.

Hans Mommsen called Hitler a "weak dictator", and Martin Broszat (The Hitler State) saw a chaos of rival agencies. Kershaw's two volumes (1998 and 2000) combine the views through "working towards the Führer".
notes.tip: Name the historian with the view: Bullock, Trevor-Roper, Taylor, Mommsen, Broszat or Kershaw. Say Hitler set the aims and took the decisions, not that he merely took part in them.

notes.h: Assessment: the Nazi state, the economy and how far Hitler caused the Second World War
notes.b: Examiners reward judgement more than narrative. For each theme, set the achievements against the limits, and be ready to weigh Hitler's own responsibility against other causes.
points: Totalitarian state: totalitarian aims and terror (SS, Gestapo, camps, courts) show control, but polycracy, a small Gestapo dependent on denunciations, and consent won by jobs and success show it was less total than it looked.
Economy, achievement: unemployment was cut, recovery was achieved and rearmament was built up.
Economy, limit: hidden unemployment, controlled wages, strain and shortages by 1939, and a recovery that had begun before 1933.
Foreign policy, achievement: by 1939 Hitler had overturned Versailles and gained territory without war.
Foreign policy, limit: it led to a general war that Germany was not ready for in 1939 and to the destruction of Germany.

Causes of the war: Hitler's aims and decisions (Mein Kampf, Hossbach, Prague, Poland) made war likely, while Versailles resentment, the weak League, appeasement, the Nazi-Soviet Pact and Mussolini shaped when and how it came.
Plan or opportunism: the usual balanced verdict is fixed long-term aims with opportunist timing and methods, which fits both Trevor-Roper's programme and Taylor's opportunism.

Munich: contemporaries felt relief and cheered Chamberlain in 1938, but it is now generally judged a failure that gave away Czechoslovakia's defences and left Hitler convinced that the western powers would not fight.
notes.tip: Take a clear position (for example, to a great extent) and argue it throughout, because narrative without judgement scores poorly. Weigh Hitler's aims against other causes.

keyTerms.definition: A system in which the state seeks to control every aspect of public and private life through a single party, secret police and propaganda.
The Nazi idea of a master race of Germanic people, used to justify racial hierarchy, persecution and the conquest of other peoples.
The Nazi goal of acquiring living space, mainly in Eastern Europe, for the German population through conquest and resettlement.
Rule by one leader or party that holds power without free elections, an independent parliament or a free press.
The Nazi policy of bringing all institutions, states and organisations into line with the party and its leadership.
The law of 23 March 1933 that allowed Hitler's cabinet to make laws without the Reichstag for four years.
British and French policy of making concessions to Germany in the 1930s to avoid war and satisfy grievances about Versailles.
The annexation of Austria by Germany on 12 March 1938.
The Nazi ideal of a racially united people's community in which class divisions would disappear and individuals served the nation.
The purge of 30 June to 2 July 1934 in which Hitler had Ernst Röhm and other SA leaders, and several political opponents, killed.
The Nazi leisure organisation, part of the German Labour Front, that offered cheap holidays and entertainment to workers.
The record of a meeting of 5 November 1937 at which Hitler outlined to his chiefs his aim of seizing living space by force.

factCards.definition: The fire of 27 February 1933 was used to justify emergency decrees that suspended civil liberties.
Passed on 23 March 1933, with only the Social Democrats voting against.

factCards.term: Night of the Long Knives: dates and victims
factCards.definition: Between 30 June and 2 July 1934 Hitler ordered the killing of Ernst Röhm, Gregor Strasser, Kurt von Schleicher and others.

factCards.term: Hindenburg's death and Hitler's new title
factCards.definition: Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934, and Hitler combined the offices of President and Chancellor as Führer.

factCards.term: Four Year Plan: date and head
factCards.definition: Announced in September 1936 under Hermann Göring, it aimed to prepare Germany for war within four years.
Hitler announced conscription and an air force on 16 March 1935, in breach of Versailles.
The January 1935 plebiscite returned the Saar to Germany with over 90 per cent voting for reunion.
German troops reoccupied the demilitarised Rhineland on 7 March 1936.
Signed on 29 to 30 September 1938 by Britain, France, Germany and Italy, it gave Germany the Sudetenland.
German troops entered Prague on 15 March 1939, and Bohemia and Moravia became a German protectorate.

factCards.term: Nazi-Soviet Pact: date and secret protocol
factCards.definition: Signed on 23 August 1939, the pact contained a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe between Germany and the Soviet Union.
Recorded at a meeting of 5 November 1937, it shows Hitler telling his chiefs that Germany needed living space and that it could be solved only by force, probably around 1943 to 1945.
Signed in June 1935, it allowed Germany a navy about 35 per cent the size of the British navy.
The leisure arm of the Labour Front, which gave workers cheap holidays and trips so that they would accept loss of free unions.
Speer became Armaments Minister in February 1942; Goebbels proclaimed total war at the Sportpalast on 18 February 1943.
Stauffenberg's bomb at Rastenburg failed to kill Hitler, and the plot was crushed with thousands of arrests.

factCards.term: Munich: handover timetable and who was excluded
factCards.definition: Czechoslovakia handed over the Sudetenland between 1 and 10 October 1938; Czechoslovakia and the Soviet Union were not at the conference.
